claim: Humans look nearly hairless compared with other apes: most human body hair is fine, short vellus hair rather than visible fur.
source_title: Peer-reviewed article on human body-hair density and its evolution (PMC3367735; a person confirms its title when opening the link)
note: Excerpt: humans have about the same follicle density as an ape of the same size 'despite our hairless appearance'; most follicles produce 'small, unpigmented vellus hairs'. 'Hardly have fur' is the appearance, which c5–c6 then explain.

sentence: Nearly every hair has its own tiny muscle, and when we're cold or frightened, a nerve tugs it, pulling the hair upright and the skin into a bump.
claim: Most body hair follicles have an arrector pili, a tiny smooth muscle attached to the follicle; when it contracts the hair stands up and the skin around it is pulled into a bump (piloerection, goosebumps).
note: Excerpt (search summary of the encyclopedia entry and the arrector pili literature): the arrector pili muscles are 'small muscles attached to hair follicles in mammals'; contraction erects the hair. 'Nearly every hair': some hairs (eyelashes, for example) have none.

sentence: Nearly every hair has its own tiny muscle, and when we're cold or frightened, a nerve tugs it, pulling the hair upright and the skin into a bump.
claim: Piloerection is an involuntary reflex driven by the sympathetic nervous system, triggered by cold or by fear (strong emotion).
source_title: What goosebumps are for (NIH Research Matters, National Institutes of Health)
note: Excerpt (NIH, Shwartz 2020 coverage): cold exposure elevates sympathetic nerve activity, triggering goosebumps; other summaries: 'triggered by sympathetic nervous activity from cold or fear'. Screen: 'sympathetic nerve'.

sentence: In a furry animal, that fluffs the coat into a blanket of trapped air.
claim: In furred mammals, erected hair traps a layer of air near the skin, which insulates and helps keep the animal warm.
source_title: Why do we get goosebumps? (Live Science)
note: Excerpt: air 'becoming trapped between the erect hairs, helping the animal retain heat'; air is a poor conductor of heat. The fur drawing is badged 'illustration'.

sentence: We have about as many hair follicles as a chimpanzee, but ours grow fine, almost invisible hairs.
claim: Humans have about the same density of hair follicles as an ape of similar body size (roughly as many as a chimpanzee).
source_title: Peer-reviewed article on human body-hair density and its evolution (PMC3367735; a person confirms its title when opening the link)
note: Excerpt: 'the human body has about the same follicle density as an ape of the same size'; a separate summary: 'roughly as many follicles as chimpanzees … the difference is in hair type rather than number'. Hedged 'about'; the evidence base is small (the paper notes a systematic cross-species study is still needed).

sentence: We have about as many hair follicles as a chimpanzee, but ours grow fine, almost invisible hairs.
claim: Most human body follicles grow vellus hairs: fine, short, unpigmented and barely visible.
source_title: Peer-reviewed article on human body-hair density and its evolution (PMC3367735; a person confirms its title when opening the link)
note: Excerpt: 'most of which produce small, unpigmented vellus hairs'; vellus hair 'virtually invisible to the naked eye'.

sentence: So the bumps look like a leftover.
claim: Goosebumps in humans are commonly described as a vestigial reflex: with sparse hair they no longer insulate or make us look bigger.
source_title: Why do we get goosebumps? (Live Science)
note: Excerpt: the reflex 'has largely lost its practical utility in humans … the insulating layer created is negligible'. The line states the common view, which the next sentence complicates.

sentence: But a team at Harvard found that nerve also reaches the stem cells that grow hair, and the muscle holds it in place.
claim: Shwartz et al. (2020, Hsu lab, Harvard) found that the sympathetic nerves that drive the arrector pili also form synapse-like contacts with hair follicle stem cells and regulate them through norepinephrine (noradrenaline).
source_title: Shwartz Y, Gonzalez-Celeiro M, Chen CL, et al., Hsu YC. Cell types promoting goosebumps form a niche to regulate hair follicle stem cells. Cell 2020;182(3):578–593.e19
note: Excerpt: 'Sympathetic nerves form synapse-like structures with HFSCs and regulate HFSCs through norepinephrine'. In mice; the screen says 'in mice · Shwartz et al., 2020'.

sentence: But a team at Harvard found that nerve also reaches the stem cells that grow hair, and the muscle holds it in place.
claim: In the same study, the arrector pili muscle maintains the sympathetic nerve's connection to the hair follicle stem cells.
source_title: Shwartz Y, Gonzalez-Celeiro M, Chen CL, et al., Hsu YC. Cell types promoting goosebumps form a niche to regulate hair follicle stem cells. Cell 2020;182(3):578–593.e19
note: Excerpt: 'APMs maintain sympathetic innervation to HFSCs'.

sentence: In the cold, that nerve wakes the stem cells, and the mice grew new hair sooner.
claim: In mice, cold exposure raised sympathetic nerve activity, which both triggered goosebumps and accelerated hair follicle stem cell activation and new hair growth.
source_title: What goosebumps are for (NIH Research Matters, National Institutes of Health)
note: Excerpt: 'Cold exposure elevates sympathetic nerve activity, triggering both goosebumps and accelerating stem cell activation and hair growth.' The voice says 'the mice'.

sentence: Take the little muscle away, and the wiring fades.
claim: When the arrector pili muscle cells were removed, the nerve–stem cell connections were lost, and stem cell activation and new hair growth were delayed (mice).
source_title: Getting goose bumps could boost hair growth (Science News)
note: Excerpt: 'Without the muscle cells, connections between the nerves and stem cells were lost, and the mice showed a delay in both stem cell activation and production of new hair.' 'The wiring fades'.

sentence: And most of the hairs it tends are thinner than a third of a sheet of paper.
claim: Vellus hairs are by definition less than 30 µm in diameter (terminal hairs are typically about 60–80 µm).
source_title: Vellus hairs on the scalp (Donovan Hair Clinic, a dermatology practice's article)
note: Excerpt: vellus hairs are 'always less than 30 micrometers in diameter'; terminal hairs 'typically 60 to 80 micrometers'. A clinic's article: a person checks it against a dermatology text before posting. 'Most of the hairs it tends' = most body follicles grow vellus hair (c6). Computed: 30 ÷ 100 = 0.3, 'thinner than a third'.

sentence: And most of the hairs it tends are thinner than a third of a sheet of paper.
claim: Standard 80 gsm copy paper is about 100 µm thick; 17 µm is about 0.17 of it ('thinner than a fifth', computed).
source_title: Papers and boards: category and standards (WJEC, UK education resource)
note: As Outer Layer No. 001's paper claim. Excerpt: copying paper 80 gsm, 100 microns. Everyday reference; not a skin claim.

sentence: Because the muscle that raises a hair still looks after it.
claim: The arrector pili muscle and its nerve, besides raising the hair, help regulate the stem cells that regenerate it (in mice).
source_title: Shwartz Y, Gonzalez-Celeiro M, Chen CL, et al., Hsu YC. Cell types promoting goosebumps form a niche to regulate hair follicle stem cells. Cell 2020;182(3):578–593.e19
note: As c8–c11 (NIH: 'what goosebumps are for'). 'Looks after it' is the image.
